title: Gaussian elimination: equivalent equations and solution structure
attribution: Original AI-assisted questions, explanations, examples, and transfer prompts for RecallWeave. General mathematical references: MIT OpenCourseWare 18.06SC, Elimination with Matrices and Solving Ax = b: Row Reduced Form R (Gilbert Strang, Fall 2011). No source exercises or figures are reproduced. Educator review is still needed.
license: Original contribution provided under the repository's applicable license; cited MIT OCW material remains under its own terms and is linked as a reference only.

items.prompt: The augmented row [2, -3 | 7] is multiplied by -2. Which new row preserves the equation?
items.explanation: Every term, including the right-hand side, is multiplied by the same nonzero number: 2x - 3y = 7 becomes -4x + 6y = -14. Scaling only one side changes the solutions.
items.transfer: Write the result of multiplying [3, 1 | -4] by 1/3. Explain why the reverse operation exists.

items.prompt: Why is multiplying a row by zero excluded from elementary row operations?
options: It makes all numbers too small.
It replaces an equation by 0 = 0 and can lose a restriction.
It always proves the system has no solution.
items.explanation: The equation x + y = 5 restricts x and y. Multiplication by zero leaves 0 = 0, which every pair satisfies. There is no inverse operation that reconstructs the lost equation.
items.transfer: Give one pair that satisfies 0 = 0 but does not satisfy x + y = 5.

items.prompt: R2 is replaced by R2 - 3R1 while R1 is kept. Which operation undoes this?
options: Replace R1 by R1 + 3R2.
Replace R2 by R2 + 3R1.
Multiply R2 by -1/3.
items.explanation: Because R1 is unchanged, adding 3R1 back to the new R2 recovers the original R2. This reversibility explains why adding a multiple of another row preserves the whole solution set.
items.transfer: Explain why simultaneously replacing both rows using already changed values needs separate, explicitly ordered steps.

items.prompt: For [0, 2 | 4; 3, 1 | 5], how can you start a pivot in the first column?
options: Divide the first row by zero.
Swap the two rows.
Declare that the system is inconsistent.
items.explanation: A zero candidate pivot does not prove inconsistency. The second row has a nonzero first entry, so swapping rows moves it into position. The system has x = 1 and y = 2.
items.transfer: What would you do if every remaining entry in a candidate coefficient column were zero?

items.prompt: Start with [1, 1 | 5; 2, -1 | 1]. After R2 ← R2 - 2R1, what is R2?
items.explanation: Compute every entry: 2 - 2(1) = 0, -1 - 2(1) = -3, and 1 - 2(5) = -9. Forgetting the right-hand side breaks equivalence.
items.transfer: Normalize the new second row, then use it to clear the entry above its pivot.

items.prompt: A row is [0, -7/3 | -11/3]. Which nonzero scale produces a leading 1?
options: Multiply by -7/3.
Multiply by -3/7.
Multiply by 3/7.
items.explanation: The reciprocal of -7/3 is -3/7. Multiplying the whole row gives [0, 1 | 11/7], exactly. The sign matters as well as the reciprocal.
items.transfer: Normalize [0, 5/2 | -3/4] without converting either entry to a decimal.

items.prompt: Which reduced augmented row proves that a system has no solution?
items.explanation: The row [0, 0 | 1] asserts 0x + 0y = 1, impossible for all x and y. A zero row adds no restriction; [1, 0 | 0] simply requires x = 0.
items.transfer: Explain why [0, 0, 0 | -4] is also a contradiction, even though its final entry is not 1.

items.prompt: The reduced system is [1, 2, -1 | 3; 0, 0, 0 | 0]. Which describes all solutions?
options: (x1, x2, x3) = (3 - 2s + t, s, t) for any real s and t.
There are no solutions because one row is zero.
items.explanation: Only x1 is a pivot variable. Let x2 = s and x3 = t; then x1 + 2s - t = 3 gives x1 = 3 - 2s + t. Two free variables produce a two-parameter family.
items.transfer: Choose s = -1 and t = 2, then check all three coordinates in the original nonzero equation.

items.prompt: A system with three variables has coefficient rank 2 and augmented rank 2. How many free variables does its solution family have?
options: Zero: equal ranks always give a unique solution.
One: it is consistent and 3 - 2 variables are free.
Two: rank directly counts free variables.
items.explanation: Equal coefficient and augmented ranks mean consistency. The number of free variables is the number of variables minus the coefficient rank: 3 - 2 = 1. Uniqueness additionally requires a pivot in every variable column.
items.transfer: How would the conclusion change if the augmented rank were 3 while the coefficient rank stayed 2?

items.prompt: Which pair satisfies both x + y = 5 and 2x - y = 1?
items.explanation: Substitute (2, 3): 2 + 3 = 5 and 2(2) - 3 = 1. Checking only the first equation would fail to distinguish all three options.
items.transfer: Check the pair obtained by solving x + y = 7 and 3x - y = 1 in both original equations.

items.prompt: A proposed row reduction of x - y = 2 and 2x - 2y = 5 claims x = 2, y = 0. What is the decisive check?
options: It satisfies the first equation, so accept it.
The second equation gives 4 rather than 5; in fact subtracting twice the first equation yields 0 = 1.
Any pair with y = 0 is invalid.
items.explanation: The candidate fails the second original equation. More strongly, R2 - 2R1 produces a contradiction, proving that no pair can satisfy both. An attractive-looking final vector cannot override the original constraints.
items.transfer: Write the linear combination of these original equations that certifies inconsistency.

items.prompt: Exact row reduction shows an observed-data system Ax = b is inconsistent. What does a least-squares problem change?
options: It finds an exact solution to the same equations by rounding a pivot.
It chooses x to minimize a stated residual objective such as the squared length of Ax - b.
It permits scaling a row by zero while preserving every original solution.
items.explanation: Least squares solves a different optimization problem when exact equality is impossible. Row operations diagnose consistency; they cannot create an exact solution to contradictory original equations. A least-squares result must be interpreted through its residuals.
items.transfer: Explain why a small residual in every measured equation is a different claim from satisfying every equation exactly.
